chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

And for any person in ihram whose shoe is lost and he does not have a pair of shoes, it is permissible for him to wear the khuff (leather socks) if he is compelled to do so, and the jorab (socks) he wears if he is compelled to wear them.
And if the person in ihram eats the meat of game without knowing what it is, a sheep's blood (dam) becomes obligatory upon him.

key_terms.الْجَوْرَبَيْنِ: The two socks (jorab), soft footwear worn under shoes
key_terms.الْخُفَّيْنِ: The two leather socks (khuff), a specific type of footwear permitted in ihram under necessity
key_terms.دَمُ شَاةٍ: A sheep (as a sacrificial expiation or dam)
key_terms.مُحْرِم: Person in the state of ihram (sacred ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.نَعْل: Shoe (specifically the upper footwear worn with sandals)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim who loses their shoes or eats game meat unknowingly during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of *darurah* (necessity) in Ihram regulations, permitting the wearing of leather socks or regular socks when proper footwear is lost, thereby balancing ritual purity with practical constraints. It further establishes the expiation (*kaffarah*) for unintentionally consuming game meat, requiring the sacrifice of a sheep, which underscores the distinction between error and deliberate transgression in Shia fiqh. These rulings are foundational in the *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* for understanding the flexibility of Ihram conditions under duress.
